summary:
An opinion piece arguing that women represent a major part of the solution to the U.S. skilled trades labor shortage. The author, writing from the perspective of a trade training provider, notes that women grew from 1.9% of U.S. electricians twenty years ago to 3.5% by 2025, and that participation is also rising in HVAC, electrical, welding and trucking.

Drivers of that shift include rising college tuition, deliberate recruitment efforts aimed at women, and the fact that many trades pay wages equal to or above some degree-requiring careers while requiring shorter training periods. Faster completion matters to employers because experienced tradespeople are retiring and replacements are needed quickly. The author frames the aging workforce as having a silver lining: it draws in groups not traditionally associated with the trades, diversifying the pipeline for women and minorities.

Barriers persist. Women still report discrimination, exclusion and harassment on job sites, plus lingering assumptions that trade work suits men better, which can shape hiring, promotion and perceptions of ability. With few women in leadership or senior trade roles, role models are scarce; the author cites the saying "you can't be what you don't see."

On what works: employers value adaptability, reliability, accountability and communication as much as technical skill. Students want assurance that training converts into real opportunity. Programs should provide career exploration, hands-on learning, employer partnerships and visible role models, and should continue support past graduation with interview prep and employer connections, since that follow-through determines success in the classroom-to-jobsite transition. The author reports that confidence grows alongside technical skill, and that graduates cite pride in meaningful work, financial stability, and opening doors for other women.

Conclusion: the trades should be presented as a legitimate first-choice career, not a backup plan, and the sector's future depends on workforce development quality rather than outdated assumptions about who belongs.

claims.claim: Women made up a small but growing share of U.S. electricians over two decades
